manti-food.name: Manti
manti-food.summary: A dumpling dish of spiced meat wrapped in dough, found across Central Asia, West Asia, the South Caucasus and the Balkans, and especially popular in Turkish cuisine.

samanu.name: Sumalak
samanu.summary: Another regional name for samanu, a sweet paste of germinated wheat and flour traditionally prepared for Nowruz, a practice traced back to the pre-Islamic Sasanian Persian Empire.

ottoman-cuisine.name: Ottoman cuisine
ottoman-cuisine.summary: The cuisine of the Ottoman Empire, which continues today in the cooking of Turkey, the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and North Africa.

pelmeni.name: Pelmeni
pelmeni.summary: Dumplings of filled dough considered Russia's national dish, with roots among the Komi and Udmurt; the name pelnan, meaning 'ear bread,' came from Finno-Ugric peoples introduced to the dish by Iranian merchants.

mahmud-al-kashgari.name: Mahmud al-Kashgari
mahmud-al-kashgari.summary: 11th-century Kara-Khanid scholar and lexicographer of the Turkic languages from Kashgar, who later settled in Baghdad as a political refugee.

timur.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
timur.summary: Turco-Mongol conqueror (1320s–1405) who founded the Timurid Empire across Central Asia and the Middle East, seen as one of history's greatest and most brutal military leaders.

timurid-dynasty.name: Timurid dynasty
timurid-dynasty.summary: The Turco-Mongol ruling family of the Timurid Empire, descended from Timur, whose members also founded the Mughal Empire and called themselves Gurkani, meaning 'son-in-law'.

timurid-renaissance.name: Timurid Renaissance
timurid-renaissance.summary: A late 14th- to early 16th-century revival of arts and sciences across the Muslim world under the Timurid Empire, including advances in astronomy and Persian art.

shah-rukh.name: Shah Rukh
shah-rukh.summary: Son of Timur (Tamerlane) who ruled the eastern Timurid Empire from 1405 to 1447, controlling Silk Road trade and making Herat his capital and a centre of art and science.

ulugh-beg.name: Ulugh Beg
ulugh-beg.summary: A Timurid ruler (1394–1449), astronomer, and mathematician who built the renowned Ulugh Beg Observatory in Samarkand during the Timurid Renaissance, before being executed after his son's revolt.

tartarium.name: Tartarium
tartarium.summary: A costly medieval luxury textile, also called cloth of Tars, made by combining various materials.

ilkhanate.name: Ilkhanate
ilkhanate.summary: A Mongol khanate established by Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, ruling Iran and neighboring lands from 1259; it converted to Islam under Ghazan and collapsed after ruler Abu Sa'id died in 1335.

zbeg-khan.name: Özbeg Khan
zbeg-khan.summary: Khan of the Golden Horde from 1313 to 1341, its longest-reigning ruler and the leader under whom the state reached its peak.

yuan-dynasty.name: Yuan dynasty
yuan-dynasty.summary: A Mongol-led dynasty ruling China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan, and the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China.

chinggisids.name: Chinggisids
chinggisids.summary: The descendants of Genghis Khan and his wife Börte, who by tradition were considered the only legitimate rulers of the Mongol Empire and its successor states, a rule that lasted until 1847.

ljait.name: Öljaitü
ljait.summary: Eighth ruler of the Ilkhanid dynasty, reigning from 1304 to 1316 in Tabriz; son of the Ilkhan Arghun and brother of Mahmud Ghazan.

soltaniyeh.name: Soltaniyeh
soltaniyeh.summary: A city in Zanjan province, Iran, serving today as capital of both Soltaniyeh County and its central district.

armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.summary: Armenian state formed in the Middle Ages by refugees fleeing the Seljuk invasion of Armenia, centered in Cilicia and a strong ally of the Crusaders; it became a kingdom in 1198.

yumurtal-k.name: Ayas (Yumurtalık)
yumurtal-k.summary: A Mediterranean port town in Adana Province, Turkey, known in the medieval period as Ayas, a Cilician Armenian harbour captured by the Mamluks in 1347.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

golden-horde.name: Golden Horde
golden-horde.summary: Mongol, later Turkicized khanate (also called the Ulus of Jochi) that split from the Mongol Empire in the 13th century and ruled from Siberia to Eastern Europe until fragmenting after 1396.

tartary.name: Tartary
tartary.summary: A vague blanket term used in European writing and maps from the 13th to 19th centuries for the largely unknown vastness of inner Asia, unconnected to any real state or people.

genghis-khan.name: Genghis Khan
genghis-khan.summary: Founder of the Mongol Empire (c. 1162-1227), who united the Mongol tribes and conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

batu-khan.name: Batu Khan
batu-khan.summary: Mongol ruler (about 1205 to 1255) and grandson of Genghis Khan who founded the Golden Horde, whose territory ruled the Kievan Rus', Volga Bulgaria, Cumania and the Caucasus for about 250 years.

subutai.name: Subutai
subutai.summary: Mongol general (c. 1175–1248) and chief military strategist for Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan, who directed over 20 campaigns and conquered more territory than any other commander in history.

shiban.name: Shiban
shiban.summary: A Mongol prince of the early Golden Horde, grandson of Genghis Khan and younger brother of Batu Khan, ancestor of the later Shaybanid dynasty.

veretskyi-pass.name: Veretskyi Pass
veretskyi-pass.summary: A mountain pass in the Carpathian Mountains in Ukraine, one of the most important routes through the range.

kalchyk-river.name: Kalka River
kalchyk-river.summary: A river in present-day Ukraine, historically known as the Kalka, site of the 1223 battle in which Mongol forces defeated a coalition of Rus' princes.

jebe.name: Jebe
jebe.summary: A prominent Mongol general under Genghis Khan (died c. 1224), originally an enemy soldier who became one of his greatest commanders and helped expand the Mongol Empire.

anushtegin-dynasty.name: Anushtegin dynasty
anushtegin-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Turkic Muslim dynasty of mamluk origin that ruled the Khwarazmian Empire across Central Asia, Afghanistan and Iran from about 1077 until the Mongol conquest in the 13th century.

mstislav-mstislavich.name: Mstislav the Bold
mstislav-mstislavich.summary: A prince of Tmutarakan and Chernigov, one of the Rus' princes of Kievan Rus' in the decades before the Mongol invasions, who died around 1228.

cumans.name: Cumans
cumans.summary: A Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia who dominated the steppe north of the Black Sea, becoming powerful warriors who influenced medieval Rus', Hungary and the Balkans.

hulegu-khan.name: Hulegu Khan
hulegu-khan.summary: Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265) and grandson of Genghis Khan who conquered much of West Asia, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia, and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid dynasty.

kitbuqa.name: Kitbuqa
kitbuqa.summary: An Eastern Christian Naiman general who served the Mongol Ilkhan Hulagu, helping sack Baghdad in 1258, and was killed in 1260 at the Battle of Ain Jalut, the first major defeat of Mongol expansion.

baybars.name: Baybars
baybars.summary: The fourth Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria (1260-1277), a former slave who defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut and campaigned successfully against the Crusaders.

qutuz.name: Qutuz
qutuz.summary: Mamluk Sultan of Egypt who reigned less than a year (1259–1260) but led the Mamluk army to a decisive victory over the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, then was assassinated on the journey home.

b-la-iv-of-hungary.name: Béla IV of Hungary
b-la-iv-of-hungary.summary: King of Hungary and Croatia from 1235 to 1270 whose army was destroyed by the Mongols at the Battle of Mohi in 1241, after which he worked to rebuild the kingdom.

battle-of-mohi.name: Battle of Mohi
battle-of-mohi.summary: An 11 April 1241 battle in which the Mongol Empire under Batu Khan destroyed the royal army of Hungary's King Béla IV, a turning point in Hungarian history.

henry-ii-the-pious.name: Henry II the Pious
henry-ii-the-pious.summary: Duke of Silesia and High Duke of Poland (1238 to 1241), a Piast prince who died leading forces against the Mongols at the Battle of Legnica in 1241.

legnica.name: Legnica
legnica.summary: A city in southwestern Poland, seat of Piast dukes for about 700 years and site of a 1241 battle where the Mongols defeated a Polish-led Christian coalition.

kadan.name: Kadan
kadan.summary: Son of Ögedei Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan, brother of Güyük Khan, who led Mongol forces attacking Poland during the Mongol invasion of Europe.

wenceslaus-i-of-bohemia.name: Wenceslaus I of Bohemia
wenceslaus-i-of-bohemia.summary: King of Bohemia from 1230 to 1253, nicknamed One-Eyed, son of Ottokar I of Bohemia.

xiangyang.name: Xiangyang
xiangyang.summary: A city in Hubei province on the Han River, formed from the once-separate Xiangyang and Fancheng, that played prominent roles in ancient and pre-modern Chinese history.

battle-of-legnica.name: Battle of Legnica
battle-of-legnica.summary: 1241 battle in which a Mongol army defeated combined Polish and Moravian forces under Duke Henry II the Pious, part of the Mongol invasion of Poland.

aqyn.name: Aqyn (akyn)
aqyn.summary: Improvisational poets and singers in Kazakh and Kyrgyz culture who compete in song battles, historically voicing people's thoughts among mostly illiterate nomadic populations.

ali-shir-nava-i.name: Ali-Shir Nava'i
ali-shir-nava-i.summary: Timurid poet, writer and statesman (1441–1501) regarded as the founder of early Turkic literature, who argued his native Chagatai Turkic surpassed Persian for poetry.

diwan-poetry.name: Diwan (poetry)
diwan-poetry.summary: Tradition of poetry collections by a single author across Islamic cultures of West and Central Asia, North Africa and South Asia, dominated by lyric forms such as ghazals.

rumi.name: Rumi
rumi.summary: Sufi mystic and poet (1207–1273) who founded the Mevlevi Order; his Masnavi is considered one of the greatest works of Persian literature.

balkh.name: Balkh
balkh.summary: A city in northern Afghanistan, historically a center of Zoroastrianism and Buddhism known to Persians as Zariaspa and Greeks as Bactra; capital of ancient Bactria, later devastated by the Mongols.

sangtuda.name: Wakhsh
sangtuda.summary: A village in present-day Tajikistan on the Wakhsh River, known simply as Wakhsh in medieval times.

konya.name: Konya (Iconium)
konya.summary: City in central Turkey known in antiquity as Iconium, later capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, and today the spiritual centre of the Whirling Dervishes.

seljuk-empire.name: Seljuk Empire
seljuk-empire.summary: A medieval Turco-Persian empire founded in 1037 by brothers Tughril and Chaghri, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia, whose 1071 victory at Manzikert weakened Byzantine control there.

ghaznavid-empire.name: Ghaznavid Empire
ghaznavid-empire.summary: Persianate Muslim empire of Turkic origin that flourished from 977 to 1186, stretching at its height from the Oxus River to the Indus Valley.

ibn-al-athir.name: Ibn al-Athir
ibn-al-athir.summary: A Hadith expert, historian and biographer of Arab descent (1160–1233) who settled in Mosul at age 21 to devote himself to the study of history and Islamic tradition.

merv.name: Merv
merv.summary: A major ancient Iranian city in Central Asia on the Silk Road, settled from the 3rd millennium BC, that at times served as capital of the caliphate and of the Great Seljuk Empire and became a center of Islamic science.

hamdallah-mustawfi.name: Hamdallah Mustawfi
hamdallah-mustawfi.summary: A 14th-century Persian official, historian, geographer and poet from Qazvin, known for works including the history Tarikh-i Guzida.

tarikh-i-guzida.name: Tarikh-i guzida
tarikh-i-guzida.summary: A compendium of Islamic history from the creation of the world to 1329, written by Hamdallah Mustawfi and completed in 1330.

komuz.name: Komuz
komuz.summary: An ancient fretless three-stringed instrument, the best-known Kyrgyz national symbol, traditionally carved from a single piece of apricot or juniper wood.

dombra.name: Dombra
dombra.summary: A long-necked plucked lute used in traditional Kazakh, Uzbek and related musics, and the principal national instrument of Kazakhstan.

khamag-mongol.name: Khamag Mongol
khamag-mongol.summary: A 12th-century tribal confederation on the Mongolian Plateau, considered a predecessor of the Mongol Empire. Its first known khan, Khabul Khan, repelled Jin invasions before his successor Ambaghai was captured and executed by the Jin.

secret-history-of-the-mongols.name: Secret History of the Mongols
secret-history-of-the-mongols.summary: The oldest surviving literary work in Mongolic languages, written for the Mongol royal family after Genghis Khan's death in 1227 to recount his life, conquests, and part of his successor's reign.

buryats.name: Buryats
buryats.summary: A Mongol ethnic group native to southeastern Siberia and northern Mongolia, traditionally regarded as the main northern branch of the Mongols and known for nomadic herding.

rashid-al-din-hamadani.name: Rashid al-Din Hamadani
rashid-al-din-hamadani.summary: Statesman, historian and physician in Ilkhanate Iran (1247–1318) who, as vizier, wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, a key source on the Mongol Empire, before being executed.

jami-al-tawarikh.name: Jami' al-Tawarikh
jami-al-tawarikh.summary: Early 14th-century work often called 'the first world history,' written by Rashid al-Din for the Mongol Ilkhanate and covering cultures from China to Europe.

ghazan.name: Ghazan
ghazan.summary: Seventh ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate (r. 1295–1304), best known for converting to Islam in 1295 and reforming the empire's currency and fiscal policy.

altan-debter.name: Altan Debter
altan-debter.summary: Early, now-lost history of the Mongols that the Persian scholar Rashid-al-Din Hamadani drew on when writing his own chronicle, the Jami al-Tawarikh.

pax-mongolica.name: Pax Mongolica
pax-mongolica.summary: A term for the stability and eased trade and communication across Eurasia under Mongol rule after Genghis Khan's conquests, lasting until the empire fragmented and the Black Death spread.

fancheng-xiangyang.name: Fancheng
fancheng-xiangyang.summary: A district of the city of Xiangyang in Hubei, China, besieged alongside Xiangyang by the Mongols from 1268 to 1273.

zhang-gui.name: Zhang Gui
zhang-gui.summary: Governor of Liang province and first Duke of Xiping under the Western Jin dynasty (255–314), whose son succeeded him as governor after his death.

bayan-of-the-baarin.name: Bayan
bayan-of-the-baarin.summary: A Mongol general of the Yuan dynasty (1236-1295) who led Kublai Khan's army to conquer the Southern Song dynasty of China.

northern-yuan.name: Northern Yuan
northern-yuan.summary: Mongol Borjigin dynastic state on the Mongolian Plateau, a rump state formed after the Yuan dynasty's collapse in 1368 and conquered by the Later Jin dynasty in 1635.

middle-mongol.name: Middle Mongol
middle-mongol.summary: A Mongolic language spoken across the Mongol Empire, originating in Genghis Khan's home region, which split into several Mongolic languages after the empire's collapse.

changzhou.name: Changzhou
changzhou.summary: A prefecture-level city on the Yangtze River in Jiangsu, China, historically known under names such as Yanling and Lanling.

thunder-crash-bomb.name: Thunder crash bomb
thunder-crash-bomb.summary: An early cast-iron gunpowder bomb or grenade developed in 12th to 13th century China during the Song and Jin dynasties.

m-ngke-khan.name: Möngke Khan
m-ngke-khan.summary: The fourth khagan of the Mongol Empire, ruling 1251–1259, who oversaw conquests of Iraq, Syria and the Dali Kingdom; his death without a successor triggered a civil war that split the empire.

toluid-civil-war.name: Toluid Civil War
toluid-civil-war.summary: A Mongol war of succession (1260-1264) between Kublai Khan and his brother Ariq Böke after Möngke Khan's death, which helped split the Mongol Empire into separate khanates.

chagatai-khanate.name: Chagatai Khanate
chagatai-khanate.summary: A Mongol khanate ruled by descendants of Chagatai Khan, Genghis Khan's second son, spanning Central Asia at its late-13th-century height before its ruling elite Turkified and adopted Islam.

barlas.name: Barlas
barlas.summary: A Mongol tribe later Turkified in Central Asia, which produced the ruling dynasties of both the Timurid Empire and the Mughal Empire.

timurid-empire.name: Timurid Empire
timurid-empire.summary: A Turco-Mongol, Persian-influenced Muslim empire founded by Timur in 1370, dominating Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan and Central Asia into the 15th century.

abu-sa-id-bahadur-khan.name: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan
abu-sa-id-bahadur-khan.summary: Ninth ruler of the Ilkhanate, the Mongol-founded state covering present-day Iran and neighboring lands, from about 1316 until his death in 1335, after which the Ilkhanate broke apart.

saray-mulk-khanum.name: Saray Mulk Khanum
saray-mulk-khanum.summary: A princess of Moghulistan and descendant of Genghis Khan (c. 1341–1408) who became chief consort of Timur, founder of the Timurid Empire.

jamukha.name: Jamukha
jamukha.summary: Leader of the Jadaran tribe who was proclaimed Gur Khan, or universal ruler, by rival factions in 1201, and Temüjin's principal opponent in the struggle to unify the Mongol tribes.

chupan.name: Chupan
chupan.summary: A Chupanid noble and nominal general of the Mongol Empire who served the Ilkhanate until his death in 1327, also honored as a duke by the Yuan emperor.

irinjin.name: Irinjin
irinjin.summary: A powerful Kerait emir serving the Ilkhanate and viceroy of Anatolia, active from about 1295 to 1319.

turco-mongol-tradition.name: Turco-Mongol tradition
turco-mongol-tradition.summary: An ethnocultural blend that arose in the 13th–14th centuries among the Mongol ruling elites of the Golden Horde and Chagatai Khanate, who adopted Islam and Turkic languages while keeping Mongol institutions.

nizari-isma-ilism.name: Nizari Isma'ilism
nizari-isma-ilism.summary: The largest branch of the Ismailis, the second-largest branch of Shia Islam, whose spiritual leader today is the Aga Khan.

rukn-al-din-khurshah.name: Rukn al-Din Khurshah
rukn-al-din-khurshah.summary: Fifth and final Nizari Isma'ili Imam at Alamut (1230–1256), who negotiated with the invading Mongols and surrendered Alamut Castle, ending Nizari rule in Persia.

maymun-diz.name: Maymun-Diz
maymun-diz.summary: A major Nizari Ismaili fortress of the Alamut period in Persia, where Imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah was residing when he surrendered to the Mongols in 1256, leading to its demolition.

alamut-castle.name: Alamut Castle
alamut-castle.summary: Ruined mountain fortress in Iran that served as headquarters of the Nizari Ismaili state from 1090 until captured by the Mongols in 1256, famed for its gardens, library and laboratories.

jani-beg.name: Jani Beg
jani-beg.summary: Khan of the Golden Horde from 1342 until his death in 1357, who took power after defeating his older brother Tini Beg following their father's death.

taqiyya.name: Taqiyya
taqiyya.summary: The Islamic practice of concealing one's faith to avoid danger, mainly associated with Shia Islam but also permitted under certain conditions in Sunni tradition.

anjedan-iran.name: Anjudan
anjedan-iran.summary: A village in central Iran near Qom and Kashan where the Nizari Ismaili Imamate relocated in the late 14th century, giving its name to the 14th- to 15th-century 'Anjedan period' of Nizari history.

ma-huan.name: Ma Huan
ma-huan.summary: Chinese Muslim explorer, translator and travel writer, about 1380 to 1460, who accompanied Admiral Zheng He on three of his voyages to the Western Oceans.

chen-cheng-ming-dynasty.name: Chen Cheng
chen-cheng-ming-dynasty.summary: A Chinese diplomat of the Ming dynasty (1365 to 1457), known for his overland journeys into Central Asia, contemporary with the admiral Zheng He's treasure voyages.

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.summary: A major city in southeastern Uzbekistan and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia, a key Silk Road center once capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Sogdiana.

abdal-latif-mirza.name: Abdal-Latif Mirza
abdal-latif-mirza.summary: Great-grandson of Timur and third son of Timurid ruler Ulugh Beg, living from about 1420 to 1450.
